strengths: The paper is generally well-written and easy to follow.
The paper provides theoretical grounds on their model and shows competitive performances compared to other baselines.
The paper provides some interesting insights on anomaly detection on tabular data with large-language models.
The paper is quite well written. It is easy to follow and logical.
Instead of simply using large LLMs, small variants are explored, and it is shown that they are no less better.
The paper introduces a novel model type for anomaly detection using a large language model.

The method provides an effective way to handle text and categorical data as features for anomaly detection, which are typically challenging to manage. To do so, they proposed a method to mitigate length-bias in the LLM’s output probabilities and theoretically validated it.
The authors demonstrate a preprocessing technique for tabular data, facilitating effective LLM fine-tuning.
The work is easy to follow and the motivation is clear.
It’s good to consider different types in tabular data, such as textual, numerical and categorical columns.
Experiment results show good potential for AnoLLM.
weaknesses: An example for anomaly detection (in Figure 1) would be good for reader's understanding of what is an anomaly detection for tabular data. (Possibly an example explicitly included in the dataset used for the experiments)

From the results, it is difficult to determine which model performs the best without explicit standard deviation (which is provided in the appendix). It would be better to have some simple plots (e.g., critical difference plots) that incorporates some statistical testing to determine which model is performing better.
While the authors state there is a similar trends for other metrics, it would be good to see the actual results (at least in the appendix), since there is a high imbalance of normal/anomaly.
The time comparison between the models and the discussion on the trade-off would be very interesting.
It is confusing to see "50% of normal samples for training" in the evaluation protocol. Clearer description would help better understanding of the experiments.

One interesting direction for the future works might be to pretrain a model suited for the anomaly detection. Moreover, more elaboration on impacts for the proposed model would be interesting for the conclusion.

It is unclear how the proposed method handles high-cardinality categorical features. Grouping rare categories might not be sufficient, and more details on this pre-processing step are needed. Furthermore, the impact of this grouping on the final results should be discussed.
The effect of number of decimal digits should have been explored in greater detail.

Similarly, the effect of normalization could have been explored in more detail. Although, the effect of raw numbers is seen, how about simply rounding raw number to x number of decimal digits (and not normalizing) to reduce effect of long decimal numbers, and then using them directly?
What is the effect of not permuting the column names, and having a canonical ordering? Are they not supposed to give even better results?
It will be good to highlight some failure cases, both false positives and false negatives, and try and analyze why that happened.
The paper claims to outperform certain deep learning methods, but some of those methods perform similarly or even better; missing baselines such as ICL and DTE should be included.
The use of column permutations may act as an ensemble strategy; baselines should also be evaluated with these same permutations for fair comparison.
Including F1-score or AUC-PR results as supplemental material would be helpful as these metrics are more sensitive to class imbalances.
The claim that AnoLLM outperforms deep learning methods should be more cautiously framed.
The computational expense of the proposed method is high (7 A100 GPUs), making it difficult for others to access or replicate, and no code is provided.
A section discussing inference and training times would help clarify this limitation.
The paper should clarify the distinction between unsupervised and semi-supervised anomaly detection, as experiments were conducted in a semi-supervised setting and Section 2.1 needs revision.
The method seems too simple and lacks novelty; using negative log likelihood for anomaly detection is straightforward.
The claim of being the first to apply LLMs to tabular anomaly detection is inappropriate; many prior works exist.
The backbone LLM is not a well-known model such as Llama, Qwen, Mistral, etc.; why authors do not use these LLMs?
The differences in contribution 3 and 4 are unclear; they seem to both discuss the experiment.
In experiments, only one dataset has text columns; more datasets with text and more attributes should be considered.
More ablation studies should be provided such as the impact of Random column permutations; case study is also missing, cannot recognize which samples are anomaly.
The formatting on line 249 could use some improvement.
